1987 Constitution on public utilities: (1) only 60% Filipino-owned corporations may operate; (2) foreign investor board participation limited to proportionate share in capital; (3) all executive and managing officers must be Filipinos
Capital stock: (a) voting shares (elect board); (b) non-voting or preferred shares (cannot elect directors but may vote on fundamental corporate changes)
Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011): majority of 10, led by Justice Carpio -- capital means only voting shares; directed SEC to apply to PLDT and impose sanctions if violation found

Gamboa minority (3 dissenters led by Justice Velasco): jurisdictional, procedural, due process issues hobble majority; capital should include all shares as interpreted since 1935; Constitution already ensures Filipino control via item 2 (foreigners can use only 40% of common shares in electing directors) and item 3 (only Filipinos as executive and managing officers)

CJ philosophy: on economic and business issues -- absent grave abuse of discretion -- courts should defer to Executive Department; on civil liberties -- scales of justice weigh heavily against government and in favor of poor and marginalized; liberty and prosperity philosophy
Most objectionable: retroactive sanction threat against investors who relied in good faith on 75-year uniform construction
If decision cannot be reversed: give investors reasonable period (a few years) to comply; Congress should pass law governing orderly and fair divestment process

stances.claim: The Gamboa majority capital = voting shares only ruling is wrong on merits -- the Constitution already ensures Filipino control through two other mechanisms: (1) foreigners can use only 40% of common shares they hold in electing directors; (2) only Filipinos may be executive and managing officers.

The most objectionable aspect of Gamboa is the retroactive threat of sanction against foreign investors who relied in good faith on the government 75-year uniform representation -- a most cruel and unfair retroactive punishment.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with Alberto Lina's (Air 21) offer to establish a 24/7 free OFW call center needing only DOLE cooperation. He then analyzes Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011), in which a majority of 10 led by Justice Carpio held that 'capital' in the public utility constitutional provision means only voting shares, directing the SEC to apply this to PLDT and impose sanctions for violations. CJ explains the 3-member minority's arguments (led by Justice Velasco): the Constitution already ensures Filipino control through two other mechanisms -- (1) foreign investors can use only 40% of common shares in electing directors, so Filipinos always control the board; and (2) only Filipinos may be executive and managing officers. He articulates his 'liberty and prosperity' philosophy: courts should defer to the Executive on economic issues (absent grave abuse of discretion) while weighing heavily in favor of the poor and marginalized in civil liberties cases. Most objectionable is the retroactive sanction threat: investors relied in good faith on the government's 75-year uniform construction since 1935, and punishing them retroactively is 'most cruel and unfair.' If the decision cannot be reversed, investors should be given a reasonable period to comply, and Congress should pass a law governing an orderly and fair divestment process.
